ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) is a group of environmental mycobacteria that cause disseminated disease in immunocompromised hosts and pulmonary infection in older adults. It is acquired from water, soil, and food, and requires a high index of suspicion for diagnosis.

sections.p: MAC comprises two related species, M. avium and M. intracellulare. They are non‑tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) that grow slowly and are resistant to standard anti‑TB drugs. In healthy people they rarely cause disease, but in HIV, chronic lung disease, or elderly patients they can be pathogenic.
b: Ubiquitous in water, soil, and biofilms
Slow growers: 2‑6 weeks on solid media
Resistant to isoniazid and rifampicin

sections.p: Acid‑fast bacilli, non‑motile, aerobic rods that form smooth, yellow‑orange colonies. They possess a thick, lipid‑rich cell wall that impairs host killing and allows intracellular survival within macrophages.
b: Acid‑fast positive (Ziehl‑Neelsen)
Can be cultured on Lowenstein‑Jensen or liquid MGIT
Molecular probes (e.g., 16S rRNA) identify MAC species

sections.p: Transmission is environmental, not person‑to‑person. Inhalation of aerosolised water droplets or ingestion of contaminated food leads to pulmonary or disseminated infection. Once inhaled, MAC is phagocytosed but survives within macrophages, spreading via the reticulo‑endothelial system.
b: Aerosol from showers, hot tubs, humidifiers
Contaminated unpasteurised milk or fruit juices
Opportunistic infection after CD4 <50 cells/µL

sections.p: MAC produces two main clinical syndromes: disseminated disease in severely immunocompromised patients (especially AIDS with CD4 <50) and chronic pulmonary disease in older smokers or those with underlying lung disease.
b: Disseminated MAC: fever, weight loss, night sweats, anemia, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy
Pulmonary MAC: chronic cough, sputum, weight loss, nodular/bronchiectatic radiographs
Rare skin, joint, or CNS involvement in immunocompetent hosts

t.b: Is the patient immunocompromised enough for disseminated MAC? <50 cells/µL indicates high risk and need for prophylaxis
What pattern of lung disease is present? Nodular bronchiectasis suggests MAC; cavitary lesions may mimic TB

sections.p: Diagnosis requires a combination of clinical suspicion, imaging, and microbiologic confirmation. A single positive culture from sputum may represent colonisation; two separate positive cultures or a sterile‑site culture (blood, bone marrow) confirm disease.
b: Two positive sputum cultures for MAC OR one positive sterile‑site culture
Acid‑fast stain + culture + molecular probe
Histopathology: granulomas with acid‑fast bacilli

t.b: Does the patient have MAC in the respiratory tract? Growth on solid media after >2 weeks confirms presence; need repeat sample to rule out colonisation
Is there disseminated infection? Positive blood culture is diagnostic in AIDS patients
Can we rapidly identify MAC species? Positive result supports diagnosis when culture unavailable

sections.p: Treat disseminated MAC with a macrolide‑based regimen plus ethambutol; add a rifamycin for severe disease. Pulmonary MAC requires a macrolide, ethambutol, and a third drug (rifampicin or fluoroquinolone) for at least 12 months after culture conversion. Prophylaxis with azithromycin is recommended for HIV patients with CD4 <50.
b: Macrolide (clarithromycin or azithromycin) – core drug, intracellular activity
Ethambutol – prevents macrolide resistance
Rifampicin or fluoroquinolone – added for severe or refractory cases
Avoid monotherapy – rapid resistance development

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams: MAC is an NTM, not TB; disseminated disease occurs when CD4 <50; diagnosis needs ≥2 positive cultures or sterile‑site isolate; macrolide‑based therapy is essential and prophylaxis is azithromycin in advanced AIDS.
b: MAC = opportunistic NTM in AIDS, CD4 <50
Two positive sputum cultures = disease; one may be colonisation
Macrolide + ethambutol = backbone of therapy

whenToSeekHelp: Fever, weight loss, night sweats, and hepatosplenomegaly in an AIDS patient
Progressive cough, haemoptysis, or respiratory failure in an elderly smoker
Severe anemia or pancytopenia with positive blood culture for MAC

faq.q: Why is MAC not treated with standard TB drugs?
faq.a: MAC is intrinsically resistant to isoniazid and rifampicin; macrolides are needed for intracellular activity.

faq.q: When should prophylaxis be started in HIV?
faq.a: When CD4 count falls below 50 cells/µL, start azithromycin weekly to prevent disseminated MAC.

faq.q: Can a single positive sputum culture diagnose MAC lung disease?
faq.a: No; at least two positive sputum cultures or one sterile‑site isolate are required to distinguish infection from colonisation.

exam: Describe the diagnostic criteria for disseminated MAC in an AIDS patient.
Explain why macrolide monotherapy should be avoided in MAC treatment.
List the key components of the standard treatment regimen for pulmonary MAC.
